turns.prompt_text: I've got this auger system built on a wooden rod On the end of the wooden rod, I've drilled two other smaller wooden rods into it I'd like to 3D print a gear to attach to this I'm going to attach it sliding it over the rod which has a diameter of 1.1 cm I am then going to thread some string through four different holes in the gear to make it tight I want to choose a gear large enough so that on the other end of the compound gear with the motor I can try either a one to two ratio, a one to three ratio or a one to four ratio where the motor is spinning faster than the auger rod Attached 1 file. - 19cf11e7-613d-4d2c-9684-446564c1dac9
turns.response_html:
Here is a strategy for designing and sizing your gear to work with the cross-dowel setup shown in the file 19cf11e7-613d-4d2c-9684-446564c1dac9.

Lashing the gear to those smaller perpendicular rods is a highly effective way to transfer torque without relying on set screws, which can easily slip on wood.

Sizing the Auger Gear

To achieve ratios of 1:2, 1:3, and 1:4 (where the motor spins faster), the large auger gear needs a tooth count evenly divisible by 2, 3, and 4.

  • Tooth Count: A 48-tooth gear is the perfect baseline. This allows you to swap out the smaller motor gear between 24 teeth (for 1:2), 16 teeth (for 1:3), and 12 teeth (for 1:4). Twelve teeth is generally the minimum recommended limit for standard 3D-printed spur gears to avoid mechanical undercutting and binding.
  • Gear Pitch (Module): A gear module of 1.5 provides robust, thick teeth that will hold up well to the torque demands of an auger.
  • Overall Size: You can calculate the pitch diameter using the formula $D = m \times z$ (where $m$ is the module and $z$ is the number of teeth). A 48-tooth gear with a 1.5 module results in a pitch diameter of 72 mm. This gives you plenty of surface area to include the lashing holes while clearing the 11 mm rod.

Attachment & Tolerances

  • Center Bore: Since your main wooden rod is 11 mm, design the center hole to be slightly oversized. When dialing in the center bore on the A1, a 0.2 mm to 0.3 mm clearance (making the hole 11.2 mm or 11.3 mm) usually yields a perfect, snug slide fit right off the build plate without needing to force or sand it.
  • Lashing Holes: Position the four holes radially around the center bore, spaced so they align directly between the four quadrants created by the smaller wooden cross-rods. This will allow the string to loop squarely over each wooden peg, pulling the gear tightly and evenly against the cross.
  • Hub Thickness: Ensure the center hub (or web) of the gear where the holes are located is at least 5 mm to 8 mm thick so the string doesn't slice through the plastic layers when under heavy torque.

turns.response_html:
Based on the image 3b865b9a-fd24-4d7a-b804-788cdd0cfe3b, that appears to be a standard 130-size hobby DC motor.

Using a smaller footprint is always ideal for infrequent, localized tasks, but there are a few mechanical realities to keep in mind when pairing this specific motor with an auger.

Motor Suitability & Torque

These 130-size motors are designed for high RPMs (often 8,000 to 15,000 RPM) but output very little torque. Augers, by nature, require substantial rotational force to overcome the friction of dragging material through a tube.

Even with a 1:4 gear reduction (which will quarter the speed and multiply the torque by roughly four), you might still find the motor stalling if the material binds. It is absolutely worth prototyping with this smaller motor first to keep the build lean, but it is a good idea to keep your larger DC motors on standby in case the auger jams.

Designing the D-Shaft Pinion Gear

To drive the auger, you will need to print a smaller pinion gear (12, 16, or 24 teeth) that mounts directly onto this motor's chamfered shaft.

  • Measuring the Bore: You will need calipers to measure two dimensions: the full diameter of the circular part of the shaft (usually 2 mm for these motors) and the thickness from the flat chamfered edge to the opposite curve.
  • Tolerances: The A1 handles tight dimensional accuracy exceptionally well. Adding just 0.1 mm to 0.15 mm of clearance to your exact shaft measurements in your CAD software should yield a tight, friction-fit D-bore that snaps onto the motor without slipping.
  • Adding a Hub: Because the 12-tooth or 16-tooth pinion gears will be physically small, there won't be a lot of plastic between the gear teeth and the center D-bore. To prevent the torque from stripping the plastic inside the hole, model a protruding cylindrical hub onto the face of the gear. This gives the motor shaft more surface area to bite into.

turns.prompt_text: It will be moving fish food While there is some friction, it is very mild and I can rotate this with my fingers with ease even with fish food However, I do not know how the behavior will change when this is filled with fish food when the feeder tank is above it I'm okay with whatever gearbox is necessary as long as it's compact enough But the primary important parts are that the motor is effectively utilized, so this gearbox is essentially translating very fast, low torque energy into very slow, high torque energy I imagine using a threaded screw gear may be appropriate here to ensure the fast speed is appropriately handled
turns.response_html:
You are exactly right. What you are describing is a worm gear drive (a worm screw on the motor driving a worm wheel on the auger), and it is the perfect solution for this exact problem.

Using a worm drive effectively bridges the gap between your small, high-speed 130-size motor and the physical demands of moving dense material from a hopper.

Here is why a worm gear is the optimal path forward:

The Advantages of a Worm Drive

  • Massive Gear Reduction in a Small Footprint: A standard single-thread worm screw driving the 48-tooth gear we discussed earlier provides an immediate 48:1 gear reduction in a single stage. This instantly converts your motor's high RPM into the slow, high-torque rotation you need, eliminating the need for a bulky, multi-stage spur gearbox.
  • Self-Locking (Non-Backdrivable): This is a critical feature for your hopper design. When the feeder tank above is full, the static weight and pressure of standard flakes or small pellets for a community tank could theoretically push against the auger blades and force it to spin when powered off, leaking food. A worm gear cannot be driven backward by the wheel; the mechanical interference acts as an automatic brake.
  • 90-Degree Layout: A worm drive requires the motor shaft to sit perpendicular to the auger rod. This allows the motor to be tucked neatly alongside or directly behind the hopper, making the entire assembly highly compact.

Handling Hopper Pressure

While turning the auger by hand feels effortless right now, the static weight of the food settling above the intake can cause compaction and friction inside the tube. The massive torque multiplier of a 48:1 worm drive will give your smaller DC motor the mechanical advantage it needs to easily chew through that resistance without stalling or overheating.

3D Printing Considerations

When modeling and slicing the worm screw for your printer, keep these factors in mind:

  • Layer Height for Smoothness: Print the worm screw vertically (standing on one end). Use a very fine layer height (e.g., 0.12 mm or 0.08 mm). The helical threads need to be exceptionally smooth; harsh layer lines will create grinding friction and wear down the mating gear quickly.
  • D-Bore Reinforcement: Since this single component will be taking the full rotational force of the motor, ensure the D-shaped bore has a thick, robust wall around it so the motor's metal shaft doesn't strip the plastic from the inside out.
  • Lubrication: Even with fine layer heights, a tiny dab of silicone grease or petroleum jelly on the worm screw will drastically reduce noise and wear between the printed parts.

Since the worm gear requires the motor to be mounted at a strict 90-degree angle to your wooden auger rod, have you thought about how you will design the structural housing to keep both parts perfectly aligned under tension?
